html:
North Korea has run political prison camps, called kwanliso, since the purges of the late 1950s, holding people accused of disloyalty, often together with their families.

Under a rule of guilt by association, up to three generations of a suspect's family could be sent away. Prisoners work in mines, farms and factories under starvation rations; many die. Survivors who escaped, such as Shin Dong-hyuk, born in Camp 14, described executions and torture. Estimates of prisoners in the 2010s ran from 80,000 to 120,000.

In 2014 a United Nations Commission of Inquiry found that the camps and other abuses were crimes against humanity, comparing them to the worst of the 20th century. The state denies the camps exist. They are part of the system of control built by Kim Il Sung and kept by Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un.
sum: North Korea has run political prison camps, called kwanliso, since the purges of the late 1950s, holding people accused of disloyalty, often together with their families.
